Collaborative Strength  
Inclusive Growth.
Over four decades ago at Shriram Finance Limited, we 
established our foundations where traditional banking fell 
short. We chose the semi-urban corridors and rural markets, 
extending credit to first-generation entrepreneurs based on 
real potential rather than rigid paperwork.
Collaborative Strength 
MUFG Bank Ltd, a member of MUFG, 
a global financial group based out 
of Japan, invested 20% stake in our 
business. Beyond the immense scale 
of this cross-border transaction, the 
alliance creates a distinct structural 
advantage. It integrates global 
institutional sophistication with 
our crystalline grassroots network, 
combining international financial 
expertise with the deep-rooted local 
trust we have spent decades building.
Inclusive Growth 
The capital and capability from this 
partnership directly reinforce our 
primary mission. By introducing global  
governance standards and advanced 
technology to India’s under-banked 
segments, we provide daily-wage workers 
and rural enterprises with the secure 
momentum necessary to achieve genuine 
economic mobility.
The framework of India’s financial services 
sector is evolving. By anchoring global 
scale within our local infrastructure, we 
harness collaborative strength to accelerate 
inclusive growth across the nation.

Partnership Update
Where Global Strength  
Meets Local Roots
Shriram Finance has completed a preferential 
allotment of Rs. 47.11 crores equity shares 
at Rs. 840.93 per share to MUFG 
Bank, a member of MUFG, a 
global financial group based out 
of Japan, valued at Rs. 39,617.98 
crores (USD 4.4 Billion) for a 20% stake in 
the Company on a fully diluted basis and placed 
Shriram Finance at the centre of one of the largest 
cross-border financial sector investments India has 
ever seen.
A significant 
milestone 
was achieved 
in the 
landscape of 
the Indian 
financial 
sector.
Two Institutions, Complementary 
Strengths
Shriram Finance brings to this partnership over four 
decades of on-ground experience: 3,225 branches spanning 
31 states and UTs, active customers and Assets Under 
Management (AUM) of more than Rs. 3 Trillion. Our 
lending model has always been built around relationship, 
the ability to assess a borrower's intent when paperwork is 
thin, to stay beside a customer through every repayment 
cycle and to show up in semi-urban and rural markets 
where formal credit has been the slowest to arrive.
MUFG Bank brings what complements this depth:  
global institutional expertise and international best practices 
across risk, governance and treasury management. 
The partnership also includes Board representation for 
MUFG Bank, which makes this less a financial transaction 
and more a long-term alignment between two institutions 
that are, in their different ways, committed to building 
something that lasts.
Capital that Opens Doors
The investment significantly strengthens our capital position 
and provides long-term growth capital across key lending 
segments. With stronger capital adequacy and greater 
balance sheet flexibility, we are positioned to accelerate 
portfolio growth in retail lending, MSME financing and 
mobility solutions, while continuing to invest in the 
technology, distribution and operational capabilities that 
scale requires.
As India's economic 
landscape matures, this 
collaboration positions 
Shriram Finance to 
participate in the 
country's next phase 
of growth, extending 
formal credit further 
into underserved 
communities, 
supporting the shift to 
cleaner mobility and 
deepening the financial 
infrastructure that 
individual enterprises 
depends on.
Numbers of that size can make 
collaboration sound abstract.
What follows is the specific 
reality behind them.

PERFORMANCE HIGHLIGHTS

Partnering with Customers
What 
One Yes Can Build
The Story of Mr. Saif, 
Chembur Branch, 15 Years
Trust is not built in a single conversation. It is built in their accumulation, in the years when things go 
well and in the years when they do not, in the moments when a lender shows up not just as a financier 
but as someone who actually knows you.
Mr. Saif's story with Shriram Finance's Chembur branch spans fifteen years of exactly that kind of trust.
When Mr. Saif first walked 
through our door, he was a 
godown labourer with one 
specific aspiration: To build a 
livelihood in the commercial 
vehicle segment. The challenge 
was equally specific. Limited 
documentation. Unstable living 
conditions. Shared rented 
accommodation. A profile that 
most institutions would have 
turned away at first glance 
without a second look.
We looked past the paperwork 
and at the person. We saw 
intent, discipline and a work 
ethic that deserved a chance. 
A 
Beginning
One 
Vehicle. 
Five 
Trucks 
with
One
and
the Odds 
against It
Beginning.
a Thriving 
Business Later
Our first association was the financing of a pre-owned commercial vehicle, 
a modest start, but one we made with full commitment. We ensured the 
process was transparent, respectful and supportive at every step, because 
we believe that every customer deserves dignity when accessing finance, 
regardless of where they are starting from.
It is a reminder that sometimes, one opportunity backed by genuine belief 
in a person can create a lifetime of progress.
Mr. Saif repaid with discipline and expanded steadily. What 
started as a single used vehicle became a logistics business 
operating five heavy trucks. His financial profile grew, and 
with it, his access to capital from multiple sources.
Yet today, despite having options, Mr. Saif continues to stay 
with us. The relationship, he says, extends past lending. It 
is built on years of trust, understanding and partnership 
through every stage of his growth.
His story reaffirms a conviction that has not changed in four 
decades: financial inclusion begins with trust, and trust, 
once earned, has a loyalty that no competing interest rate 
can easily undo.

PARTNERING WITH CUSTOMERS

Partnering with Employees
The People Who   
Built the Business
These two journeys, in their beginnings, reflect the same 
conviction: that Shriram Finance has always been built by 
people who believe what the institution believes.
The Story of  
Mr. V. Muruganandapandian, 
Deputy Managing Director, 
Joined as Trainee, 1990
Some careers are about climbing. Mr. V. 
Muruganandapandian's was about going deeper, into 
the Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns of Tamil Nadu where 
the idea of formal credit was, for most borrowers, 
still theoretical.
He started as a trainee in 1990. What he found was not 
just a job. He found a philosophy: that no dream is too 
small to fund, if the person carrying it has the intent 
and integrity to see it through.
Micro-Loans, Massive Impact
He pioneered micro-loans as small as Rs. 10,000, 
structured with a manageable daily repayment of  
Rs. 100, for grassroots collectives whose work was real 
but whose paperwork was non-existent. These included 
the Pookattuvor Sangam: flower garland makers 
whose income arrived in small, daily amounts; and the 
Poojarigal Sangam: temple priests who served their 
communities faithfully but held no salary slips.
These were hardworking individuals who lacked the 
documents traditional lending required. They did not 
lack the character to repay.
A Rs. 2 Lakhs loan extended years ago nurtured an 
aspiring entrepreneur into the proud proprietor of the 
3-star hotel chain in Tiruvannamalai. Similar trust 
fuelled the rise of powerloom operators in Tiruppur 
and established jewellers across the state. Thousands of 
truckers who came to Shriram with nothing but a drive 
to succeed now command multi-crore turnovers.
Leading the Way He Was Taught
Today, Mr. Muruganandapandian leads a business unit of 
10,000 colleagues. He credits his team for every milestone 
and ensures accountability and recognition always travel 
together, because the culture he built his career in is one 
of shared success, and he has no intention of changing 
that now.
His advice for those entering the organisation is both 
simple and demanding: Know Your Customer. Prioritise 
their welfare over pure business metrics. Communicate 
constantly, because trust is earned in conversation. And 
spend real time in sales, because that is exactly where 
lasting relationships are built.
A Culture of Decentralised Ownership
What captivated him most was how Shriram ran its 
branches. A branch manager here carried the autonomy 
and accountability of a localised CEO. Decisions were 
made by people closest to the customer, not sent down 
from the centre. That grassroots-up philosophy runs 
directly through how Mr. Jilani manages operations 
today. No major strategy is designed in an ivory tower. 
It is built on real-time inputs from frontline teams 
who understand the customer’s reality better than any 
dashboard can capture.
The Legacy He Is Building
Seeing the young professionals he once mentored now 
leading pivotal roles across Shriram Finance brings him 
greater satisfaction than any title. His counsel for those 
entering the field remains consistent: master your sector 
with absolute rigour, value long-term growth over a flashy 
starting package and never stop learning. The moment 
you stop is the precise moment you start falling behind.
Composure as a Leadership Tool
More than three decades of difficult moments 
have sharpened rather than softened his resolve. 
His approach in a crisis has never changed: gather 
complete data, set the ego outside the room, consult 
the team and calm a frantic environment through 
composure rather than volume. He has found 
consistently, that the leader who stays steady in the 
chaos is the one the team rallies around.
The Story of Mr. G.M. Jilani, 
Joint Managing Director 
& Chief Operating Officer, 
Joined as Management 
Trainee, 1992
Mr. G.M. Jilani is an architect of scale. He is also, 
equally, someone who has never lost sight of the 
individual customer at the centre of every number 
he manages.
When he stepped into Shriram Chits as a 
management trainee in Andhra Pradesh back in 
1992, he found an organisation that matched his 
own sensibilities. He quickly saw that financial 
instruments at Shriram were never abstract 
corporate transactions. They were interwoven with 
human milestones: a daughter’s wedding, a child’s 
college admission, the first commercial vehicle a 
man would call his own.

Partnering with Communities
When Finance Goes    
All the Way
Anath’s Road Back to Health
Shriram Seva Sankalp Foundation | Mobile Medical Unit Initiative
At 59, Anath Ruidas, a daily-
wage driver from Malickpur 
in West Bengal’s Hooghly 
district, spends long hours 
on the road to support his 
wife and two sons. As the 
sole breadwinner of the 
family, earning a livelihood 
often took priority over his 
own health.
For nearly four years, 
Anath had been living with 
Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus 
and hypertension. Limited 
financial resources, irregular 
health monitoring and 
the distance to medical 
facilities made consistent 
treatment difficult. As 
his symptoms worsened, 
including persistent skin 
irritation, managing 
his condition became 
increasingly challenging.
Everything changed on October 10, 2025, when Anath 
noticed a Mobile Medical Unit (MMU) implemented 
through Shriram Seva Sankalp Foundation (SSSF) while 
making a delivery in Singur. Learning that the MMU 
provided free healthcare services for drivers and their 
families, he decided to visit the camp.
Following a comprehensive health check-up, the MMU team 
recorded an RBS level of 170 mg/dL and blood pressure of 
136/71 mmHg. Along with free medicines, Anath received 
counselling on diet, exercise and lifestyle changes, supported 
by regular follow-up visits in his community.
Giving Women the Wheel 
A driving training CSR initiative empowering women with skills, independence and sustainable income, from Mathura to 
Ujjain to Thanjavur, ‘Six women. Six journeys’. that illustrate what ‘Collaborative Strength. Inclusive Growth.’ looks like when 
it happens at the most personal level.
Shriram Finance built a programme that gave them a steering wheel and the skills to hold it. In their own words:
"Before joining the Parkham

WHY INVEST IN SHRIRAM

Chairman’s Message
Collaborative Strength 
Inclusive Growth
Dear Stakeholders,
The true identity of Shriram Finance lies 
in its deep grassroots engagement, over 
four decades, across India’s underserved 
credit landscape. From the very beginning, 
the institution was built on a simple belief: 
traditional lending systems often overlook 
hardworking individuals and small enterprises 
when formal documentation does not fit 
standard institutional expectations and 
processes. With this understanding, we 
shaped a relationship-led lending model 
and built a network of 3,225 branches where 
entrepreneurial aspirations first take shape.
Our frontline teams work closely with communities every day in 
semi-urban neighbourhoods where emerging entrepreneurs need 
lenders who recognise their potential, in rural markets where a 
tractor loan can transform a farming family’s future, and in urban 
centres where daily-wage earners and small business enterprises 
gain access to formal credit for the first time. Over the years, this 
enduring local presence has helped us build a retail credit franchise 
serving 97.3 Lakhs active customers.
A borrower base of this scale is more than a business milestone; it 
reflects the power of inclusive growth. It demonstrates how access 
to finance at the grassroots level can steadily evolve into a resilient 
and trusted network, capable of supporting communities through 
changing economic conditions. This strong on-ground momentum 
also positioned us to actively participate in India’s broader 
economic growth during the financial year.
A Macroeconomic Catalyst for Scale
Globally, the year was marked by persistent inflationary pressures, 
volatile energy markets, and geopolitical uncertainties, leading 
global GDP growth to moderate to 3.1%. Despite these external 
challenges, India continued to demonstrate remarkable economic 
resilience and remained one of the key drivers of global growth.
Supported by strong public infrastructure investment, healthy 
domestic consumption, and a steadily formalising economy, India’s 
real GDP expanded by 7.7% in FY 2025-26. These structural 
strengths created meaningful opportunities for our diversified 
lending model and enabled us to further bridge the credit gap for 
underserved communities. Small road transporters, commercial 
vehicle operators, MSMEs, and self-employed individuals 
continued to rely on us as a trusted financial partner, contributing 
collectively to the nation’s economic progress.
Financial Proof of Resilient Expansion
The combination of a strong domestic economy and our 
time-tested relationship model translated into another year of 
disciplined and resilient growth. Driven by healthy credit demand 
across geographies, total Assets Under Management (AUM) 
crossed the landmark milestone of Rs. 3 Lakh Crores, reaching  
Rs. 302,274 Crores during the year.
Profitability remained strong, with Profit After Tax rising to  
Rs. 9,998 Crores and Net Interest Income increasing to  
Rs. 26,051 Crores. These results reflect our ability to grow 
responsibly while maintaining pricing discipline and operational 
efficiency. Asset quality also remained stable, with Gross Stage 
3 assets at 4.58% and Net Stage 3 assets at 2.33%. In recognition 
of this balance sheet strength, our long-term debt instruments 
received an upgraded AAA/Stable rating from major credit 
rating agencies.
At the same time, we accelerated our digital transformation 
journey by strengthening our credit architecture with AI-enabled 
identity verification and Account Aggregator data integration. 
These initiatives led to a considerable reduction in underwriting 
turnaround time (TAT), improvement in agreement execution TAT 
and reduction in loan disbursment TAT, ensuring that technology 
continues to enhance, rather than replace, our signature 
human touch.
The Realisation of Collaborative Strength
This financial year also marked a defining milestone in our 
journey, where decades of grassroots credibility converged with 
global institutional partnership.
In a significant alignment of institutional legacies, our decades of 
domestic execution came together with the rich global banking 
heritage of MUFG Bank, spanning nearly one hundred and 
forty-seven years. The preferential allotment of 47.11 crores equity 
shares of the Company at Rs. 840.93 per share to MUFG Bank was 
completed on April 08, 2026. 
This strategic cross-border investment, valued at approximately  
Rs. 39,618 Crores (USD 4.4 Billion), resulted in MUFG Bank 
acquiring a 20% stake in the Company on a fully diluted basis, 
making it one of the largest strategic transactions in India’s 
financial services sector.
More importantly, the partnership reflects a strong strategic 
alignment between two institutions with complementary 
strengths. It brings together global institutional capability and local 
market understanding, further strengthening our ability to serve 
customers effectively. Our experience across 31 states and UTs is 
now complemented by international best practices in governance, 
risk management, and access to a wider global capital ecosystem.
Together, this partnership creates a stronger and more future-ready 
financial institution, one that carries the trust of millions of Indian 
borrowers while benefiting from the confidence and expertise of 
a leading global banking group. It is a powerful example of global 
strength meeting local roots.
Advancing the Future of Shared Prosperity
The strategic capital and long-term partnership now position us 
strongly for the next phase of inclusive growth. We will continue 
expanding both our physical and digital reach across rural and 
semi-urban India, ensuring that access to finance remains a 
meaningful catalyst for livelihoods, mobility, and entrepreneurship.
At the same time, we are steadily scaling our commitment to 
future-ready mobility solutions. Our green financing portfolio 
is growing towards a targeted AUM of over Rs. 5,000 Crores, 
supporting electric commercial vehicles, two-wheelers, and clean 
energy adoption beyond metropolitan centres, while contributing 
to India’s transition towards a lower-carbon economy.
Although the near-term global environment continues to require 
caution amid geopolitical and inflationary pressures, our approach 
remains firmly anchored in prudence, diversification, and 
balance sheet resilience. With the support of an expanded Board, 
the dedication of our frontline teams, and the strength of our 
global partnership, we step into the next chapter with confidence 
and optimism.
Our commitment remains unchanged to support individual 
enterprises, strengthen families and communities, and contribute 
meaningfully to India’s entrepreneurial growth story.
With Best Regards,
Jugal Kishore Mohapatra

Carbon Emissions Management
The Company has advanced its environmental reporting 
and emissions management practices across its operational 
footprint of 3,225 branches and offices. Supported by 
enhanced digitised data collection and monitoring systems, 
the Company has improved visibility, transparency, and 
reporting efficiency across environmental performance 
indicators. During FY 2025-26, the Company achieved a 
10% reduction in energy intensity per rupee of turnover 
and a 13% reduction in Scope 1 and Scope 2 emission 
intensity per rupee of turnover. These improvements 
reflect continued progress towards operational efficiency 
and lower-carbon operations.
Recognising the significance of value chain emissions 
within the financial services sector, the Company continues 
to strengthen Scope 3 emissions assessment and reporting 
across: 
Category 1: Purchased Goods and Services
Category 2: Capital Goods
Category 3: Fuel and Energy-Related Activities 
Category 5: Waste Generated in Operations 
Category 6: Business Travel 
Category 7: Employee Commuting
Category 15: Financed Emissions 
The Company reports financed emissions in alignment 
with the Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials 
(PCAF) methodology, strengthening transparency and 
climate-related disclosures across its financing portfolio. 
During FY 2025-26, the financed emissions assessment 
covered over 80% of the Company’s lending portfolio. The 
financed emission intensity declined by approximately 
4%, from 98 tCO₂e/Rs. Crores of AUM in FY 2024-25 
to 94 tCO₂e/Rs. Crores of AUM in FY 2025-26. This 
improvement was driven by strong portfolio growth and 
an increasing allocation of financing towards lower-carbon 
assets, particularly electric vehicles.
Resource Efficiency
The Company continues to strengthen resource efficiency 
and environmentally responsible operational practices 
across its establishments. Increasing adoption of electronic 
documentation, e-signature solutions, and paperless 
processes has contributed to a reduction in paper 
consumption, supporting more efficient resource utilisation. 
The Company has also enhanced energy efficiency 
through deployment of LED lighting systems, high-
efficiency air conditioning systems, inverter-based power 
backup solutions, and use of eco-friendly biodegradable 
materials for branding and promotional activities. Further 
strengthening responsible resource management, water 
meters were installed at selected locations to improve

DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS
GLOBAL ECONOMIC OVERVIEW
Global growth is estimated at 3.4% in 2025, with a slight 
moderation to 3.1% in 2026 before stabilising at 3.2% in 
2027. This reflects a phase of steady expansion, supported 
by easing inflation and sustained investments in technology, 
even as trade policy uncertainties and evolving geopolitical 
dynamics continue to shape the broader economic landscape. 
Despite ongoing global challenges, growth remains resilient, 
supported by policy measures and continued momentum in 
private sector investment.
Navigating an Uncertain Landscape
The prolonged Russia-Ukraine conflict continued to unsettle 
energy markets, commodity flows, and agricultural trade, 
particularly affecting Europe’s energy dynamics. The Middle 
East witnessed escalating tensions since late February, with 
the conflict around Iran disrupting shipping through the 
Strait of Hormuz and raising concerns over other critical trade 
corridors, including Red Sea routes. Meanwhile, strategic 
rivalry between the United States and China resulted in tariff 
wars, tighter technology controls, and competition over 
critical minerals. This accelerated supply chain restructuring 
through friend-shoring and near-shoring strategies.

Beyond major power rivalries, instability across several 
emerging markets is compounding pressures on global 
trade, investment, and capital flows. Sanctions are changing 
trade dynamics, increased defence expenditure is redefining 
priorities, and shifting global alliances are reshaping 
engagements. In this environment, businesses are promptly 
evaluating their sourcing models, investment strategies, and 
long-term geographic exposure. Moreover, the realignment 
of the geopolitical landscape is driving economies to boost 
domestic manufacturing capabilities, expand clean energy 
initiatives, strengthen electric mobility ecosystems, and 
accelerate digital infrastructure, as new trajectories evolve 
for medium-term growth. 
Gradual Easing of Inflation
Inflationary pressures are easing, reinforcing the outlook 
for stable expansion. Global headline inflation is expected 
to decline from 4.1% in 2025 to 3.8% in 2026 and further 
to 3.4% by 2027. This trend is supported by moderating 
commodity prices, particularly energy and easing supply-
side constraints. However, the pace of disinflation is expected 
to remain uneven, with some major economies returning to 
target levels more gradually than others.
Road Ahead
Global economic conditions are expected to remain steady 
over the near term, supported by stable domestic demand in 
several economies and easing inflationary trends. The IMF 
projects global growth at 3.1% in CY 2026 and 3.2% in CY 
2027, while inflation is expected to moderate further from 
4.1% in CY 2025 to 3.8% in CY 2026 and 3.4% in CY 2027.
However, the pace of expansion is likely to remain below 
long-term trends, reflecting the continued impact of trade 
policy changes, tariff-related developments and geopolitical 
factors on global trade and investment flows. The trajectory 
of growth and inflation will remain dependent on the stability 
of energy prices, evolving policy responses and the absence 
of significant supply-side disruptions, shaping the overall 
economic environment in the coming period.
INDIAN ECONOMIC OVERVIEW
India continued to stand out as a key anchor of global growth, 
registering a GDP of 7.7% in FY 2025-26. The strength of 
the economy remains rooted in domestic demand, with 
consumption and investment together providing a stable 
growth base. Private consumption remains the primary 
driver, supported by rising real incomes, stable employment 
conditions, and improving rural and urban demand. 
Favourable agricultural output and policy measures, 
including tax rationalisation, have further strengthened 
household spending, enabling consumption to remain steady 
despite external uncertainties. 
Investment Momentum and Infrastructure Push
Investment activity has remained firm, with Gross Fixed 
Capital Formation, holding at a healthy share of GDP. Public 
capital expenditure, particularly in infrastructure, continues 
to crowd in private sector participation and reinforce 
medium-term growth. Additionally, improving business 
sentiment and capacity expansion across sectors are also 
reinforcing this momentum.
Easing Inflation and Monetary Support
India’s macroeconomic environment has become increasingly 
supportive of growth. Inflationary pressures have eased 
significantly, with headline CPI inflation averaging around 
1.7% during April-December, FY 2025-26, aided by softer 
food prices and stable supply conditions. In response, the 
Reserve Bank of India kept the repo rate unchanged at 
5.25% as of June 2026, reflecting a calibrated approach to 
supporting growth while keeping inflationary pressures 
under watch. This moderation has provided room for a more 
accommodative monetary stance, with policy measures 
aimed at supporting liquidity, lowering borrowing costs, and 
enhancing credit flow across sectors.
Prudent Fiscal Management

enabled the Government to sustain capital spending while

reinforcing confidence and supporting broad-based growth. 
Even amid a challenging global backdrop marked by trade 
disruptions and financial volatility, India’s domestically 
driven growth model, supported by policy stability and 
structural strength, continues to provide  resilience and 
visibility to the outlook.

INDIAN FINANCIAL SERVICES SECTOR OVERVIEW
India’s financial services sector entered FY 2025–26 on a 
stronger and more stable footing, underpinned by resilient 
economic activity, sustained credit demand and a more 
balanced interest rate environment. The central bank has 
highlighted that the banking system remains well-capitalised 
and adequately liquid, even as credit and deposit growth 
normalised from the elevated levels seen in the previous year.
Financial Inclusion Driving Expansion
Structural drivers such as financial inclusion and digital 
adoption continued to reinforce sectoral momentum. The 
RBI’s Financial Inclusion Index improved to 67 in 2025, 
reflecting broader access to formal financial services. At the 
same time, India’s digital payments ecosystem maintained 
its rapid expansion, with total transactions reaching 22,831 
Crores in FY 2024–25. UPI remained a key enabler of this 
transformation, recording 20,394 Million transactions 
in February 2026 alone, underscoring its central role in 
everyday financial activity and the ongoing shift towards a 
less-cash economy.
Additionally, the sector maintained a strong focus on 
prudence and risk management. 
Policy Support with Regulatory Vigilance
Policy discussions around enhancing credit access for small 
businesses, including proposals to increase collateral-free 
loan limits, signal continued support for inclusive growth. 
However, regulatory guidance and supervisory assessments 
also emphasised the need for caution in select lending 
segments, particularly within non-bank financial institutions 
where pockets of stress have emerged. Overall, India’s 
financial services sector continues to play a pivotal role in 
supporting economic expansion, while adapting to evolving 
credit dynamics, accelerating digital transformation and a 
progressively strengthening regulatory framework.

INDUSTRY SCENARIO AND FINANCING
The Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) sector 
has emerged as a vital pillar of India’s financial ecosystem, 
complementing the traditional banking system by expanding 
credit access across underserved and niche segments. Over 
the past two decades, NBFCs have demonstrated strong and 
sustained growth in assets under management (AUM) and 
credit disbursement, driven by rising demand across retail, 
MSME, infrastructure and consumer financing. By 2025, the 
sector’s total assets had reached approximately Rs. 45 Trillion, 
reflecting its deepening role in India’s credit landscape and its 
increasing relevance in bridging structural financing gaps.
Sustained Growth Momentum
NBFCs are expected to continue outpacing traditional 
bank credit growth, with loan books projected to expand 
at a healthy 15–17% through FY 2025–26. This growth 
momentum is underpinned by their ability to operate in 
specialised niches, adopt agile underwriting models, and 
leverage digital distribution channels to penetrate deeper 
into underbanked markets. Their focus on segments such 
as small business financing, vehicle loans, consumer credit, 
microfinance and co-lending partnerships with banks and 
fintech players has significantly strengthened financial 
inclusion across rural, semi-urban and urban geographies. 
The integration of technology, particularly through digital 
lending platforms, has further accelerated credit delivery, 
enabling faster onboarding and broadening access to formal 
finance for millions of borrowers. However, the sector’s 
rapid expansion, particularly in unsecured lending segments 
such as small-ticket personal loans, fintech-originated 
credit and certain microfinance portfolios have introduced 
emerging asset quality pressures. Rising delinquencies in 
these segments highlight the need for calibrated growth 
and stronger risk frameworks. In response, the regulatory 
landscape has evolved significantly, with the Reserve Bank 
of India introducing the Scale-Based Regulatory (SBR) 
framework to enhance oversight, strengthen governance 
standards, and align prudential norms with the systemic 
importance of NBFCs. This framework ensures that larger 
and more complex entities maintain robust capital adequacy, 
liquidity buffers and risk management practices, while also 
extending supervisory attention to smaller NBFCs.
Way Forward
The medium-term outlook for the sector remains 
constructive yet balanced. As per CRISIL, NBFC AUM is 
expected to grow at a mid-teen rate through FY 2026–27, 
potentially surpassing Rs. 50 trillion, supported by strong 
consumption demand and the ongoing formalisation of 
credit in the economy. At the same time, factors such as 
elevated funding costs, intensifying competition and tighter 
regulatory compliance requirements may exert pressure on 
margins. Continued investments by corporates and fintech 
players in digital lending ecosystems are also likely to reshape 
the competitive landscape. Overall, while the Indian NBFC 
sector remains structurally resilient and well-positioned 
for growth, its long-term sustainability will depend on 
disciplined underwriting, prudent capital management and 
close alignment with an evolving regulatory environment.

COMMERCIAL VEHICLE (CV)
The Indian Commercial Vehicle segment achieved its 
highest-ever sales of 1.08 Million units in FY 2025–26, 
recording growth of 12.6% year-on-year, supported by 
robust freight demand, lower financing costs following 
repo rate reductions, GST 2.0 reforms, and sustained public 
infrastructure spending. Export momentum remained 
strong, with volumes rising 17.4% to 0.095 Million units, 
driven by continued demand from neighbouring countries 
and the Middle East. Beyond volume growth, the automotive 
sector is also undergoing a structural transformation, with 
increasing emphasis on efficiency, reliability, safety and 
technological advancement. A pivotal trigger came in 
September 2025 with the reduction in GST rates from 28% 
to 18%, which lowered upfront vehicle costs and unlocked 
deferred fleet purchases.  
(Source: https://www.siam.in/news-&-updates/press-releases/auto-industry-
performance-of-q4-jan--march-2026-fy-2025-26/605)
PASSENGER VEHICLE (PV)
The Passenger Vehicle segment achieved its highest-ever 
sales of 4.64 Million units in FY 2025–26, registering growth 
of 7.9% year-on-year, supported by GST rationalisation, 
personal income tax relief, lower financing costs following 
RBI repo rate cuts, and improving consumer sentiment. 
Export performance was equally strong, reaching a record 
0.90 Million units, up 17.5%, driven by sustained demand 
across key international markets, including the Middle East, 
Africa and Latin America. 
(Source: https://www.siam.in/news-&-updates/press-releases/auto-industry-
performance-of-q4-jan--march-2026-fy-2025-26/605)
TWO-WHEELER (2W) AND THREE WHEELER (3W)
The Two-Wheeler segment surpassed its previous peak to 
achieve record sales of 21.7 Million units in FY 2025–26, 
registering growth of 10.7%, supported by improving urban 
consumption, rising discretionary spending, GST 2.0 reforms, 
and increasing electric vehicle adoption. Export performance 
remained equally strong, with volumes reaching an all-time 
high of 5.18 Million units, up 23.4% over FY 2024–25, driven 
by expanding product portfolios, growing global acceptance 
of Indian brands, strong product quality and favourable 
currency dynamics. Three Wheelers recorded domestic sales 
of 836,231 units in FY 2025-26, registering a 12.79% year-on-
year growth.
The growth trajectory, however, has been uneven across the 
year, with strong spikes during festive and seasonal periods 
and softer retail trends in some months due to weather 
disruptions and purchase deferment. Structurally, scooters 
and entry-level motorcycles continued to anchor volumes, 
while electric two-wheelers saw gradual but steady adoption, 
indicating a transition phase rather than rapid disruption. 
Overall, FY 2025-26 can be characterised as a stable growth 
year with improving fundamentals, though the pace remains 
moderate and partly policy-supported rather than a full 
cyclical boom.
(Source: https://www.siam.in/news-&-updates/press-releases/auto-industry-
performance-of-q4-jan--march-2026-fy-2025-26/605)
TRACTOR AND FARM EQUIPMENT
India’s tractor and farm equipment sector has witnessed 
a strong upswing in FY 2025–26, underpinned by robust 
demand fundamentals and favourable policy support. 
Tractors achieved domestic sales of 1,050,077 units in 
FY 2025-26 against 883,095 units in FY 2024-25, reflecting 
an 18.95% year-on-year increase. According to ICRA, the 
industry’s wholesale volume growth outlook has been sharply 
revised upward to 15–17%, compared to an earlier estimate 
of 8–10%. The momentum marks a significant acceleration 
from the modest 7% growth recorded in FY 2024–25, 
reflecting a broad-based recovery in rural demand and farm 
sector sentiment. 
The growth has been supported by a combination of policy 
interventions and favourable agricultural conditions. The 
reduction in GST on tractors to 5% has played a pivotal role 
in improving affordability, leading to price reductions of 
approximately Rs. 40,000 to Rs. 100,000 across horsepower 
categories and thereby stimulating demand. Additionally,

CONSTRUCTION EQUIPMENT
India’s construction equipment (CE) segment is expected 
to expand from USD 8.55 Billion in 2025 to USD 9.24 
Billion in 2026, reaching approximately USD 13.61 Billion 
by 2031, implying a CAGR of about 8.05% over 2026–2031. 
This growth trajectory is primarily supported by large-scale 
public infrastructure programmes, particularly the National 
Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP), a multi-trillion-dollar initiative 
driving demand across earthmoving, road construction 
and material handling equipment. According to the Indian 
Construction 
Equipment 
Manufacturers’ 
Association 
(ICEMA), construction equipment sales moderated in 
FY 2025-26, declining by approximately 2% year-on-year to 
136,995 units from 140,191 units in FY 2024-25. At the same 
time, the implementation of stricter CEV Stage V emission 
norms from 2025 is accelerating the shift towards cleaner 
and more efficient machinery, while localisation efforts are 
helping reduce supply chain dependencies and moderate 
import costs.
The National Infrastructure Pipeline spans thousands of 
projects across transport, energy, and urban infrastructure, 
creating a strong and sustained equipment demand pipeline. 
This has already translated into tangible industry growth, 
with equipment sales rising sharply in FY 2023–24, led by 
earthmoving machinery and road construction equipment. 
Large infrastructure corridors such as the Delhi-Mumbai 
Industrial Corridor and Bharatmala Phase I continue to 
anchor demand, particularly for excavators, backhoe loaders, 
and compactors, given their central role in highway and 
logistics network expansion. The broad-based nature of 
these investments ensures demand visibility across multiple 
equipment categories and geographies.
Policy-driven initiatives like Bharatmala Pariyojana and PM 
Gati Shakti have further transformed the sector by accelerating 
project 
execution 
and 
improving 
inter-ministerial 
coordination. The rapid rollout of highway construction 
under Bharatmala, alongside synchronised infrastructure 
planning under PM Gati Shakti, has significantly boosted 
demand for specialised road construction equipment such 
as asphalt pavers and motor graders. Additionally, regional 
shifts in infrastructure spending, particularly towards the 
North-East, along with mining sector reforms and the rise of 
equipment rental platforms are expanding market access and 
supporting long-term growth across both large contractors 
and smaller players.

MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (MSMES)
Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) form a 
vital pillar of India’s economic base, driving employment, 
production, and exports. With over 7.47 Crore enterprises 
employing around 32.82 Crore people, the sector is the second 
largest contributor after agriculture and remains central to 
livelihoods, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas. As per 
the Union Budget 2026–27, MSMEs contribute about 35.4% 
of manufacturing output, 48.58% of exports, and 31.1% of 
GDP, highlighting their importance in industrial growth, 
trade competitiveness, and balanced regional development.
To boost the sector’s growth, the Government has focused 
on improving formalisation, credit access, and market 
integration through initiatives such as credit guarantee 
schemes, digital lending, and Udyam registration. Additional 
support via export promotion, cluster development, and 
production-linked incentives is helping MSMEs scale 
and integrate into value chains. Alongside this, increasing 
adoption of technology, digital tools, and skill development is 
enhancing productivity and innovation, positioning MSMEs 
as key drivers of inclusive and sustainable economic growth.
(Source: https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.
aspx?PRID=2228306&utm)
GOLD LOAN
India’s gold market underwent a structural shift in FY 
2025-26 as elevated prices reshaped demand patterns 
and moved the market away from its traditional 
consumption-led model. According to the World Gold 
Council, total gold demand declined by around 11% to 
nearly 711 tonnes in 2025, primarily due to weaker jewellery 
purchases in price-sensitive segments. Despite lower volumes, 
the overall value of demand remained strong, supported by 
sharply higher prices. Additionally, gold imports rose 1.6% 
year-on-year to about USD 58.9 Billion, reflecting resilient 
underlying demand.
Global factors played a pivotal role in this reset. The 
Economic Survey of India noted a nearly 98% surge in gold 
prices during 2025, driven by a weaker US dollar, low real 
interest rates, and heightened geopolitical uncertainties. That 
environment boosted gold’s appeal as a safe-haven asset, 
with investment demand accounting for over 40% of total 
consumption. FY 2025–26 therefore marked recalibration 
rather than contraction, with the Indian gold market 
transitioning towards a more balanced mix of consumption 
and investment-led demand.

Warning Signals (EWS) to establish a robust system for

outlines governance structures, key indicators and reporting 
mechanisms to ensure timely identiﬁcation and mitigation

investors are shared with brokers and branch oﬃcials 
through whom retail debt was placed, enabling them to 
personally approach customers and inform them of the 
maturity of their investments.

contacts investors directly using the phone numbers 
provided, to notify them of matured investments.

through social media platforms to increase awareness 
among depositors.
6.   Website Disclosure – A list of unclaimed accounts, 
including details such as name, address, and amount, is 
updated annually on the Company’s website.
7.   Auto Renewal/Refund Options – Depositors are 
provided with the option of auto renewal or auto 
refund at the time of application. Deposits marked 
for auto renewal continue to be renewed on maturity, 
subject to valid KYC, in accordance with the depositor’s 
instructions.

oﬀered multiple online options to renew or refund their 
deposits through the Company’s website, e-mail, and 
WhatsApp, ensuring convenience and accessibility.

Te Mobile Medical Unit (MMU) Program aimed to provide comprehensive primary healthcare support to truck

(Internal Ombudsman for Regulated Entities) Directions,

Board had appointed Mr. K. Ravi (General Manager (Retd.)

a detailed half-yearly Internal Ombudsman Report on 
grievances/complaints received through Regulatory and 
other means. Te Internal Ombudsman suggested certain 
improvements to reduce the customer complaints/grievances 
through various initiatives undertaken by the Company 
during the Financial Year.
Te RBI had issued a notiﬁcation dated January 17, 2025, 
emphasizing the beneﬁts of nomination facility for ﬁxed 
deposit holders. Accordingly, the Company has implemented 
proactive measures to reach out to depositors/joint depositors 
to emphasize the importance of nomination(s) to simplify 
the claim settlement in the event of the depositor’s death.
Te Company had  initiated the “DAKSH” customer awareness 
campaign through key initiatives such as awareness on cyber-
crime reporting, promoting safe banking practices/digital 
fraud awareness, observing Grievance Redressal Day etc, 
by leveraging social media, SMS, email, website and Branch 
network. Te Company reviews and monitors the status of 
nomination coverage on an ongoing basis and reports the 
progress quarterly, through DAKSH Portal.
Te Company has laid down comprehensive Customer 
Grievance Redressal Mechanism Policy, duly approved by the 
Board, which provides a robust framework for the eﬀective 
and timely resolution of customer grievances. Tis policy 
is accessible to customers through the Company’s website, 
mobile application and branch network.
An eﬀective grievance redressal mechanism has been 
implemented, supported by multiple online and oﬄine 
customer touchpoints to enable seamless complaint 
registration and resolution. All customer complaints and 
service requests received through various channels are 
systematically recorded, tracked and monitored to ensure 
timely resolution and enhance customer experience. A 
specialized team manages customer complaints with 
diligence and impartiality, ensuring that unresolved issues 
are escalated through successive levels of oversight, thereby 
strengthening governance and accountability. Complaints 
received through various channels are also reported on the 
RBI’s CMS portal in line with regulatory guidelines.
Customers may initially approach the frontline grievance 
team, which is empowered to resolve most issues promptly.

Dividend is the payment made by a Company to its 
shareholders in the form of distribution of its proﬁts. Te 
proﬁts earned by the Company can either be retained 
in business and used for acquisitions, expansion or 
diversiﬁcation, or it can be distributed to the shareholders. 
Te Company may choose to retain a part of its proﬁts and 
distribute the balance among its shareholders as dividend. 
Tis Dividend Distribution Policy (‘Policy’) aims to reconcile 
between all these needs in accordance with the applicable 
laws. 
Te objective of this Policy is to ensure a regular dividend 
income for the shareholders and long term capital 
appreciation for all shareholders of the Company. Te 
Company would ensure to strike the right balance between 
the quantum of dividend paid and the amount of proﬁts 
retained in the business for various purposes. Te Board 
of Directors (Board) will refer to the Policy while declaring 
interim dividend(s)/recommending ﬁnal dividend. Trough 
this Policy, the Company would endeavour fairness, 
consistency and sustainability while distributing proﬁts to 
the shareholders. 
Tis Policy also stipulates the process for recommendation/
declaration of dividend(s) and its pay-out by the Company 
in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 
2013 (‘the Act’), SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (‘Listing Regulations’), 
guidelines issued by Reserve Bank of India (‘RBI’) and other 
rules, regulations etc. as applicable to the Company.
Class of Shares
Te Company has issued only Equity Shares and no 
Preference shares issued by the Company are outstanding.
Category of Dividends
Te Act provides for two forms of Dividend- Final and 
Interim. Te Board shall have the absolute power to declare 
interim dividend during the Financial Year, as and when they 
consider it ﬁt. Normally, the Board will endeavour to declare 
an interim dividend afer ﬁnalization of quarterly ﬁnancial 
accounts. Te Board may declare interim dividend based on 
proﬁts of the Company, one or more times in a Financial Year 
as and when considered appropriate, in line with this policy. 
Afer the audited ﬁnancial statements are approved, the Board 
may recommend ﬁnal dividend to the shareholders for their 
approval in the Annual General Meeting of the Company. 
In the event the Board declares more than one interim 
dividend in a Financial Year, the Board may recommend to 
the shareholders to treat the last interim dividend as a ﬁnal 
Dividend.
Recommendation/Declaration of Dividend
Subject to the provisions of the Act, the Board shall 
recommend/declare/pay the Dividend only out of -
i) 
Current ﬁnancial year’s proﬁt:
a) 
afer providing for depreciation in accordance with 
law and setting oﬀ carried over previous losses and 
depreciation not provided in previous year(s), if 
any.
b) 
afer transferring to reserves such amount as 
may be prescribed under the Act or applicable 
law, regulations, norms or as may be otherwise 
considered appropriate by the Board at its 
discretion.
ii) 
Te proﬁts for any previous ﬁnancial year(s):
a) 
afer providing for depreciation in accordance with 
law; 
b) 
remaining undistributed; or
iii) out of i) & ii) both.
iv)  out of free reserves in the manner permissible under the 
Act. 
Factors to be considered while declaring Dividend
Te decision regarding dividend is a crucial decision as it 
determines the amount of proﬁt to be distributed among 
shareholders and amount of proﬁt to be retained in business. 
Te Board will endeavour to take a decision with an objective 
to enhance shareholders wealth and market value of the 
shares. However, the decision regarding dividend is subject 
to several factors and hence any optimal policy in this regard 
may be far from obvious. Te Board considers a stable 
dividend to constitute an important element of the Company’s 
investment attractiveness and shareholder return. Te 
Company is classiﬁed as Investment and Credit Company by 
RBI, operates in rapidly developing, yet a volatile market. Te 
Company’s primary need is to maintain suﬃcient resources 
and ﬁnancial ﬂexibility to meet ﬁnancial and operational 
requirements. Te Company continually seeks ways to create 
shareholder value through both commercial and ﬁnancial 
strategies, which may include both organic and inorganic 
development as well as the Company’s capital management 
practices. 
Te Shareholders of the Company may not expect dividend 
for a ﬁnancial year(s) in the circumstances of challenging/
sluggish market conditions, tough liquidity position, losses 
or inadequate proﬁts.

Te Board, while considering the proposals for dividend, 
will also take into account the supervisory ﬁndings, if any, 
of the RBI on divergence in classiﬁcation and provisioning 
for Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) and qualiﬁcations, if 
any, in the Auditors’ Report to the ﬁnancial statements of 
the Company or emphasis of matter by the statutory auditor 
that indicates an overstatement of net proﬁt. In case the net 
proﬁt for the relevant period includes any exceptional and/or 
extra-ordinary proﬁts/income, the net proﬁt shall be suitably 
adjusted to exclude such extra-ordinary items for computing 
dividend pay-out ratio.
Te decision regarding recommendation/declaration of 
dividend will depend upon various external and internal 
factors including the following:
External Factors:-
State of Economy- in case of uncertain or recessionary 
economic and business conditions, the Board will endeavour 
to retain larger part of proﬁts to build up reserves to absorb 
future shocks. 
Capital Markets- when the markets are favourable, dividend 
pay-out can be liberal. However, in case of unfavourable 
market conditions, Board may resort to a conservative 
dividend pay-out in order to conserve cash outﬂows. 
Statutory and Contractual Restrictions- Te Board needs to 
keep in mind the restrictions imposed under the Companies 
Act and any other laws, the regulatory developments with 
regard to declaration of dividend, the Company’s contractual 
obligations under the loan agreements/debenture trust deed 
and other agreements, documents, writings limiting/putting 
restrictions on dividend pay-out.
Internal Factors:- 
Apart from the various external factors aforementioned, the 
Board will take into account various internal factors while 
recommending/declaring Dividend, which inter alia will 
include- 
(B) Other factors
 
i) 
Proﬁts earned during the year;
ii) 
Present and future capital requirements of the 
existing businesses;/capital expenditures and the 
Company’s debt position;
iii) Business Acquisitions opportunities;
iv) Expansion/Modernization of existing businesses;/
growth opportunities available to the Company;
v) 
Long term growth plans of the Company;
vi) Additional investments in subsidiaries/associates 
of the Company;
vii) Fresh investments into external businesses;
viii) Cash ﬂow from operations;
ix) Cost of raising funds;

Process for approval of Payment of Interim and Final 
Dividend
 
Te Company will give prior intimation of atleast 2 
working days in advance to Stock Exchanges (excluding 
the date of intimation and the date of the Board meeting) 
of date of Board Meeting in which the declaration/
recommendation of dividend will be considered.
 
Te Company will inform about the decision taken by 
Board regarding dividend to Stock Exchange within 30 
minutes of the closure of the Board Meeting.
 
Te Company will ﬁx Record date for the purpose of 
determination for list of shareholders eligible to receive 
dividend.
 
Te Company shall recommend or declare dividend at 
least 5 working days (excluding the date of intimation 
and the record date) before the record date is ﬁxed for 
the purpose.
 
Te intimation for ﬁxing Record date shall be given 
to exchange at least three working days in advance 
(excluding the date of intimation and the record date).
In the event of any amendment in SEBI (Listing Obligations 
and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 or 
any other applicable law with respect to the process of 
recommendation/approval/payment of dividend, the same 
shall prevail and shall be deemed to form part of this policy. 
Te Company stands committed to deliver sustainable value 
to all its stakeholders. Te Company will strive to distribute 
an optimal and appropriate level of the proﬁts earned by 
it in business with the Shareholders’ funds in the form 
of dividend. As explained in the earlier part of this Policy, 
determining the dividend pay-out is dependent upon several 
factors, both internal to a business and external to it. Taking 
into consideration the aforementioned factors the Board may 
consider maintaining a Dividend Pay-out ratio in the range 
of 20-25% of the proﬁts afer tax (PAT), subject to applicable 
regulations. However, the Board may amend the pay-out 
range, whenever considered appropriate by it, keeping in 
mind the aforesaid factors having a bearing on the dividend 
pay-out decision, subject to maximum dividend payout 
ratio of 50%. However, if the Company does not meet the 
applicable prudential requirement prescribed above for each 
of the last three ﬁnancial years, may be eligible to declare 
dividend, subject to a cap of 10 percent on the dividend 
payout ratio, provided the Company complies with the 
following conditions:
(a)  meets the applicable minimum capital adequacy 
requirement in the ﬁnancial year for which it proposes 
to pay dividend; and
(b)  has net NPA of less than 4 per cent as at the close of the 
ﬁnancial year.
Te Dividend Payout Ratio is the ratio between the amount 
of the dividend payable in a year and the net proﬁt as per the 
audited ﬁnancial statements for the ﬁnancial year for which 
the dividend is proposed. 
Manner of Payment of dividend 
Te Company shall use any of the electronic mode of payment 
facility approved by the Reserve Bank for the payment of the 
dividends. 
Transfer of Unpaid/Unclaimed Dividend and Equity 
Shares to Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF)
As per section 124(5) of the Companies Act, the dividend 
which remains unpaid/unclaimed for a period of seven (7) 
consecutive years or more from the date of transfer to unpaid 
dividend account shall be transferred by the Company to 
IEPF.
Utilisation of Retained Earnings
Te Retained earnings strengthen the Company’s net owned 
funds. It will further help in maintaining Capital Adequacy 
Ratio (CAR) for Non-Banking Financial Companies 
(NBFCs) in the growth phase. Te Board from time to time 
will decide utilization of the retained earnings depending 
upon various factors including organic/inorganic growth 
strategies of the Company, market competition, creating long 
term shareholder value etc. Te Board will ensure judicious 
balancing of these factors in the interest of the Company and 
its stakeholders.
Reporting Requirements
Te Company shall report details of dividend declared during 
the ﬁnancial year as per the prescribed format in Annex I of 
Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – 
Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 
2025 issued by RBI on November 28, 2025, as updated from 
time to time within a fortnight afer declaration of dividend 
to the Regional Oﬃce of the Department of Supervision of 
the Reserve Bank, under whose jurisdiction the Company is 
registered. 
Review

Regulations and Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking

periodically for additions, deletions, changes or alterations 
in the parameters, process of recommendation/declaration/

I am pleased to present the BRSR of Shriram Finance Limited (SFL) for FY2025-26, reﬂecting our continued commitment 
towards responsible growth, sustainable ﬁnance, and inclusive development. As one of India’s leading NBFCs, we remain 
focused on delivering accessible and dependable ﬁnancial solutions across commercial vehicles, passenger vehicles, 
two-wheelers, MSME ﬁnance, gold loans, personal loans, and other retail lending segments, particularly catering to 
underserved and underbanked communities across the country.
We recognise our responsibility to promote sustainable ﬁnance while reducing the environmental impact of our 
operations. In line with this commitment, the Company continues to strengthen ﬁnancing towards alternate fuel vehicles, 
electric vehicles, roofop solar systems, renewable energy technologies, and other green assets. We have also accelerated 
digitisation across operations to reduce paper consumption, adopted energy-eﬃcient infrastructure including LED 
lighting and eﬃcient air-conditioning systems, and implemented resource conservation initiatives such as water-saving 
measures at selected locations. Further, the Company continues to strengthen its assessment of ﬁnanced emissions and 
integrate climate considerations into its business practices to support a more sustainable future.
At Shriram Finance Limited, we understand the signiﬁcance of social responsibility and the impact of communities on 
our shared future. To this end, we have undertaken initiatives to support education, healthcare, and skill development 
for underprivileged sections of society. We are proud to announce that we have provided scholarships to more than 
4,96,000 underprivileged children from various regions in the country. Furthermore, our preventive healthcare program 
for truckers has established mobile medical units across 15 locations in 11 states, beneﬁting over 16,25,000 trucking 
community at large. In addition, we have trained and upskilled more than 1,60,000 truck drivers and 6,600 youth from 
disadvantaged backgrounds were trained in the ﬁeld of Automotive Two-Wheeler repair & services. 
Strong governance practices continue to remain central to our business approach. We are committed to maintaining 
high standards of ethics, transparency, accountability, and responsible business conduct through robust governance 
frameworks, eﬀective risk management practices, and strong compliance mechanisms. Our commitment to employee 
well-being is reﬂected through comprehensive beneﬁts, including life, health, and accidental insurance, along with 
continuous learning and development opportunities. During FY2025-26, we undertook a Double Materiality Assessment 
to identify and prioritise key ESG issues based on both their ﬁnancial impact on the business and the Company’s impact 
on society and the environment. 
As we move ahead, we remain steadfast in our commitment to integrating ESG principles into our strategy and operations 
while creating long-term value for all stakeholders. We believe that responsible ﬁnancing, inclusive growth, and sustainable 
business practices will continue to guide our journey towards building a resilient and future-ready organisation.

 Provide details of instances of engagement with, and actions taken to, address the concerns of vulnerable/marginalised 
stakeholder groups: 
 
 Trough its Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives, the Company undertakes various programs focused on 
supporting and empowering marginalized, vulnerable, and underserved communities. To assess the eﬀectiveness and 
outcomes of its programs, the Company has undertaken comprehensive CSR impact assessments for the following:
 
(A) Regular Scholarship Program
Description: Te program provides merit-based ﬁnancial assistance to students from transport-industry families to 
support uninterrupted education from Classes 8 to 12.
Impact: Te scholarship program addressed a critical ﬁnancial need for students from economically vulnerable 
households, enabling continued access to education and improved academic outcomes. Around 85% of beneﬁciaries 
reported improvement in academic performance, while 100% of students were able to continue their schooling afer 
receiving the scholarship. Te program also contributed towards greater educational inclusion, with 87% of respondents 
observing increased participation of girls in continuing their education.
Sustainability: Te program promotes long-term educational continuity and enhanced career opportunities for 
students from economically vulnerable households, contributing to sustained socio-economic development.
 
(B) Mobile Medical Unit (MMU) Program
Description: Te MMU Program provides accessible primary healthcare services, including consultations, diagnostics, 
medicines, health screenings, and awareness program to the drivers of the trucking community and their families 
through mobile healthcare units deployed at key transport hubs.
Impact: Te program signiﬁcantly enhanced healthcare accessibility and health outcomes within the trucking 
community. Beneﬁciaries reported high levels of satisfaction with the services, reduced out-of-pocket healthcare 
expenditure, and improved management of chronic health conditions, highlighting the programme’s role in promoting 
preventive healthcare and continuity of care. 
Sustainability: Te program promotes sustained health and well-being through improved access to primary healthcare, 
preventive health awareness, early diagnosis and management of chronic conditions, contributing to enhanced quality 
of life for the trucking community and their families.
 
(C) Two Wheeeler Automotive Program
Description: Te program provides industry-relevant skill training in two-wheeler repair and servicing to 
underprivileged and unemployed youth, along with placement support to enhance employability and sustainable 
livelihood opportunities in the automotive sector.
Impact: Te program delivered strong employability and livelihood outcomes, with 78.22% of participants securing 
employment and 87.1% obtaining placements within three months of training completion. Participants also reported 
signiﬁcant improvement in practical and hand-on skills, particularly in servicing and repair functions, enhancing 
workplace readiness and resulting in long-term livelihood opportunities. Te program has made early progress through 
women only batches and dedicated mobilizations eﬀorts and female enrolment grown steadily over the years. 
Sustainability: Te program promotes long-term economic empowerment by developing practical skills and creating 
sustainable employment pathways, enabling youth from underserved communities to achieve economic self-reliance 
and career growth.

Describe the mechanisms in place to receive and respond to consumer complaints and feedback: 
Te Company has established a comprehensive grievance redressal framework to eﬀectively manage customer complaints 
and feedback.
 
Nature of Complaints:
Customer grievances generally relate to matters such as non-receipt of deposit/debenture certiﬁcates, non-credit of interest 
amounts, discrepancies in investor details, non-updation of address, non-receipt of dividends or maturity proceeds, non-
receipt of account statements or No Objection Certiﬁcates (NOCs), and other related concerns. Complaints pertaining 
to services provided by agents or intermediaries engaged by the Company are also addressed under this framework, with 
appropriate oversight maintained on Lending Service Provider and other service providers.
 
Complaint Management System:
Te Company utilises a centralised Customer Service Management System (CSMS) to record, track, and resolve customer 
grievances received through multiple channels, including call centres, branch oﬃces, head oﬃce, oﬃcial website, and the 
Company’s mobile application. All customer interactions and issues are systematically logged in to the CSMS for timely 
action and resolution.
 
Modes of Lodging Complaints:
Customers may register their complaints or service requests through the following channels:
• 
Telephonic communication with the call center, branches, or oﬃces 
• 
Email to designated customer care or grievance redressal email IDs 
• 
Submission through the Company’s oﬃcial website or mobile application 
 
Redressal Process and Escalation Mechanism:
All complaints received through various channels are recorded in the CSMS and addressed by the respective regional teams. 
In the event of delays or unsatisfactory resolution, an escalation framework is in place:
• 
Level 1: Regional Team Leader 
• 
Level 2: Zonal Team Leader 
• 
Level 3: Head – Geographical Units (Commercial) 
 
Grievance Redressal Oversight:
Te Grievance Redressal Oﬃcer (GRO) oversees the complaint resolution process. Te Company endeavors to resolve all 
customer complaints within a maximum period of 30 days from the date of receipt.
If a customer does not receive a response within the stipulated timeframe or is dissatisﬁed with the resolution provided, they 
may escalate the matter to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) through the RBI CMS Portal or the RBI Contact Centre.
Complaints received from regulatory authorities, including the RBI, are routed to designated Nodal Oﬃcers for resolution.

1. 
In conjunction with our audit of the Standalone 
Financial Statements of Shriram Finance Limited (the 
“Company”) as at and for the year ended March 31,

Management’s Responsibilities for Internal Financial 
Controls
2. 
Te Company’s Management is responsible for 
establishing and maintaining internal ﬁnancial controls 
based on the internal ﬁnancial controls with reference 
to Standalone Financial Statements criteria established 
by the Company considering the essential components 
of internal control stated in the Guidance Note on 
Audit of Internal Financial Controls over Financial 
Reporting (the “Guidance Note”) issued by the Institute 
of Chartered Accountants of India (“ICAI”). Tese 
responsibilities include the design, implementation and 
maintenance of adequate internal ﬁnancial controls that 
were operating eﬀectively for ensuring the orderly and 
eﬃcient conduct of the Company’s business, including 
adherence to the Company’s policies, the safeguarding 
of its assets, the prevention and detection of frauds and 
errors, the accuracy and completeness of the accounting 
records, and the timely preparation of reliable ﬁnancial 
information, as required under the Act.
Auditor’s Responsibility for the Audit of the Internal 
Financial Controls with Reference to Standalone Financial 
Statements 
3. 
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the 
Company’s internal ﬁnancial controls with reference to 
Standalone Financial Statements based on our audit. We 
conducted our audit in accordance with the Guidance 
Note and Standards on Auditing issued by the ICAI 
prescribed under Section 143(10) of the Act, to the 
extent applicable to an audit of internal ﬁnancial controls 
with reference to Standalone Financial Statements. 
Tose Standards and the Guidance Note require that we 
comply with ethical requirements and plan and perform 
the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether 
adequate internal ﬁnancial controls with reference to 
Standalone Financial Statements were established and 
maintained and if such controls operated eﬀectively in 
all material respects.
4. 
Our audit involves performing procedures to obtain 
audit evidence about the adequacy of the internal 
ﬁnancial controls with reference to these Standalone 
Financial Statements and their operating eﬀectiveness. 
Our audit of internal ﬁnancial controls with reference to 
Standalone Financial Statements includes obtaining an 
understanding of such internal ﬁnancial controls with 
reference to these Standalone Financial Statements, 
assessing the risk that a material weakness exists, 
and testing and evaluating the design and operating 
eﬀectiveness of internal control based on the assessed 
risk. Te procedures selected depend on the auditor’s 
judgement, including the assessment of the risks of 
material misstatement of the Standalone Financial 
Statements, whether due to fraud or error.
5. 
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is 
suﬃcient and appropriate to provide a basis for our audit 
opinion on the Company’s internal ﬁnancial controls 
with reference to Standalone Financial Statements.
Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to 
Standalone Financial Statements 
6. 
A Company’s internal ﬁnancial controls with reference 
to Standalone Financial Statements is a process 
designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the 
reliability of ﬁnancial reporting and the preparation of 
Standalone Financial Statements for external purposes 
in accordance with generally accepted accounting 
principles. A Company’s internal ﬁnancial controls 
with reference to Standalone Financial Statements 
include those policies and procedures that (1) pertain 
to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable 
detail, accurately and fairly reﬂect the transactions and 
dispositions of the assets of the Company; (2) provide 
reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded 
as necessary to permit preparation of Standalone 
Financial Statements in accordance with generally 
accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and 
expenditures of the Company are being made only in 
accordance with authorisations of management and 
directors of the Company; and (3) provide reasonable 
assurance regarding prevention or timely detection

Company’s assets that could have a material eﬀect on

Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial Controls with

7. 
Because of the inherent limitations of internal ﬁnancial 
controls with reference to Standalone Financial 
Statements, including the possibility of collusion or 
improper management override of controls, material 
misstatements due to error or fraud may occur and not 
be detected. Also, projections of any evaluation of the 
internal ﬁnancial controls with reference to Standalone 
Financial Statements to future periods are subject to the 
risk that the internal ﬁnancial controls with reference 
to Standalone Financial Statements may become 
inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the 
degree of compliance with the policies or procedures 
may deteriorate.

as at March 31, 2026, based on the internal ﬁnancial 
controls with reference to Standalone Financial 
Statements criteria established by the Company 
considering the essential components of internal control 
stated in the Guidance Note issued by the ICAI.

date and instead requires that the said right should exist on the reporting date and have substance. Te amendment also 
introduces guidance on classiﬁcation of liabilities with covenants. Te Company being a NBFC, has no impact of these

not have any signiﬁcant impact in its ﬁnancial statements.

temporary mandatory relief from deferred tax accounting for top-up tax and require companies to disclose that they 
have applied the relief. Tis relief is immediate and applies retrospectively. Te amendments also require companies to 
provide new disclosures to compensate for potential loss of information resulting from the relief. Such disclosures are to be 
provided for annual reporting periods beginning on or afer April 01, 2025. Te Company has reviewed the amendment 
and based on its evaluation has determined that it does not have any signiﬁcant impact in its ﬁnancial statements.

MATERIAL ACCOUNTING POLICIES
Te material accounting policies related to preparation of the standalone ﬁnancial statements are given below:
     6.1 Financial instruments
Initial recognition
I  Classiﬁcation of ﬁnancial instruments
Te classiﬁcation depends on the contractual terms of the cash ﬂows of the ﬁnancial assets and the Company’s business 
model for managing ﬁnancial assets which are explained below:
 
 
a) 
Business model assessment
 
 
 
 Te Company determines its business model at the level that best reﬂects how it manages groups of ﬁnancial assets 
to achieve its business objective. Te Company’s business model is not assessed on an instrument by instrument 
basis, but at a higher level of aggregated portfolios and is based on observable factors such as:
 
 
 
• 
 How the performance of the business model and the ﬁnancial assets held within that business model are 
evaluated and reported to the Company’s key management personnel.
 
 
 
• 
 Te risks that aﬀect the performance of the business model (and the ﬁnancial assets held within that business 
model) and the way those risks are managed. 
 
 
 
• 
 How managers of the business are compensated (for example, whether the compensation is based on the fair 
value of the assets managed or on the contractual cash ﬂows collected).
 
 
 
• 
 Te expected frequency, value and timing of sales are also important aspects of the Company’s assessment. 
Te business model assessment is based on reasonably expected scenarios without taking ‘worst case’ or ‘stress 
case’ scenarios into account. If cash ﬂows afer initial recognition are realised in a way that is diﬀerent from the 
Company’s original expectations, the Company does not change the classiﬁcation of the remaining ﬁnancial 
assets held in that business model, but incorporates such information when assessing newly originated or 
newly purchased ﬁnancial assets going forward.
 
 
 
• 
 At initial recognition of a ﬁnancial asset, the Company determines whether newly recognised ﬁnancial assets 
are part of an existing business model or whether they reﬂect the commencement of a new business model. 
Te Company reassesses its business models each reporting period to determine whether the business models 
have changed since the preceding period. 
 
 
 
 For the current and prior reporting periods, the Company has not identiﬁed a change in its business model.
 
 
b) 
Te Solely Payments of Principal and Interest (SPPI) test

II  
Derivatives
 
  
A derivative is a ﬁnancial instrument or other contract with all three of the following characteristics:
 
  
 
• 
 Its value changes in response to the change in a speciﬁed interest rate, ﬁnancial instrument price, commodity price, 
foreign exchange rate, index of prices or rates, credit rating or credit index, or other variable, provided that, in the 
case of a non-ﬁnancial variable, it is not speciﬁc to a party to the contract (i.e. the underlying).
 
  
 
• 
 It requires no initial net investment or an initial net investment that is smaller than would be required for other 
types of contracts expected to have a similar response to changes in market factors.
 
  
 
• 
It is settled at a future date.
 
  
 The Company enters into derivative transactions with various counterparties to hedge its foreign currency risks and 
interest rate risks. Derivative transaction consists of hedging of foreign exchange transactions, which includes interest 
rate and currency swaps, interest rate options and forwards. The Company undertakes derivative transactions for 
hedging on-balance sheet liabilities.  
 
  
 Derivatives are recorded at fair value and carried as assets when their fair value is positive and as liabilities when their 
fair value is negative. The notional amount and fair value of such derivatives are disclosed separately. Changes in the fair 
value of derivatives are included in net gain on fair value changes.
 
  
Hedge accounting
  
Te Company has adopted hedge accounting. Te Company makes use of derivative instruments to manage exposures to 
interest rate risk and foreign currency risk. In order to manage particular risks, the Company applies hedge accounting for 
transactions that meet speciﬁed criteria. Te Company has formally designated and documented the hedge relationship to 
which the Company wishes to apply hedge accounting and the risk management objective and strategy for undertaking 
the hedge. Te documentation includes the Company’s risk management objective and strategy for undertaking hedge, the 
hedging/ economic relationship, the hedged item or transaction, the nature of the risk being hedged, hedge ratio and how 
the Company would assess the eﬀectiveness of changes in the hedging instrument’s fair value in oﬀsetting the exposure to 
changes in the hedged item’s cash ﬂows attributable to the hedged risk. Such hedges are expected to be highly eﬀective in 
achieving oﬀsetting changes in cash ﬂows and are assessed on an on-going basis to determine that they actually have been 
highly eﬀective throughout the ﬁnancial reporting periods for which they were designated. 
  
Hedges that meet the criteria for hedge accounting and qualify as cash ﬂow hedges are accounted as follows: 
Cash ﬂow hedge
 
  
 A cash ﬂow hedge is a hedge of the exposure to variability in cash ﬂows that is attributable to a particular risk associated with

cost in the statement of proﬁt and loss. When the hedged cash ﬂow aﬀects the statement of proﬁt and loss, the eﬀective portion 
of the gain or loss on the hedging instrument is recorded in the corresponding income or expense line of the statement of

Overview of the ECL principles
 
  
 
 Te Company records allowance for expected credit losses for all loans and other ﬁnancial assets not held at FVTPL in 
this section all referred to as ﬁnancial instruments. Equity instruments are not subject to impairment under Ind AS 109 
- Financial Instruments.
 
  
 
 Te ECL allowance is based on the credit losses expected to arise over the life of the asset (the lifetime expected credit 
loss), unless there has been no signiﬁcant increase in credit risk since origination, in which case, the allowance is based 
on the 12-months expected credit loss.
 
  
 
 Lifetime ECL are the expected credit losses resulting from all possible default events over the expected life of a ﬁnancial 
instrument. Te 12-months ECL is the portion of Lifetime ECL that represent the ECLs that result from default events 
on a ﬁnancial instrument that are possible within the 12 months afer the reporting date.
 
  
 
 Both Lifetime ECLs and 12-months ECLs are calculated on either an individual basis or a collective basis, depending 
on the nature of the underlying portfolio of ﬁnancial instruments. Te Company has grouped its loan portfolio into 
commercial vehicles, construction equipment, farm equipment, passenger vehicles, gold loan, personal loans, MSME 
secured, MSME unsecured, two-wheeler and loans to NBFC.
 
  
 
 Te Company has established a policy to perform an assessment, at the end of each reporting period, of whether a 
ﬁnancial instrument’s credit risk has increased signiﬁcantly since initial recognition, by considering the change in the 
risk of default occurring over the remaining life of the ﬁnancial instrument. Te Company does the assessment of 
signiﬁcant increase in credit risk at a borrower level. If a borrower has various facilities having diﬀerent past due status, 
then the highest Days Past Due (DPD) is considered to be applicable for all the facilities of that borrower.
